summary: This standards-track memo defines RSVP-TE extensions for creating backup label-switched paths, which protect LSP tunnels by allowing local repair. Traffic can be redirected in tens of milliseconds after a failure. It defines two methods, one-to-one and facility backup.

eli5.summary: If a bridge closes, you want a ready detour that traffic can switch to instantly. This protocol sets up such detours in advance.

questions: difference between one-to-one and facility backup
what is a point of local repair
what is the rsvp detour object
subtitle: Pre-built detours for MPLS tunnels, so traffic can switch around a failed link or router in tens of milliseconds.

tldr.problem: When a link or router on an MPLS traffic-engineered tunnel fails, waiting for path computation and failure signaling to reach the head-end is too slow for real-time traffic such as voice over IP.
tldr.mechanism: Backup tunnels are computed and signaled in advance, and the router next to the failure (the point of local repair) switches traffic onto them. Two methods are defined, one-to-one detours and facility bypass tunnels, using new FAST_REROUTE and DETOUR objects in RSVP.
tldr.outcome: Redirection is aimed at tens of milliseconds because no computation or signaling is needed after the failure. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8271, RFC 8537, RFC 8796 and RFC 9705.

today: RFC 4090 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8271, RFC 8537, RFC 8796 and RFC 9705; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Local Repair
sections.content:
RFC 4090 extends RSVP to set up backup label-switched path (LSP) tunnels for the local repair of LSP tunnels. The target is real-time applications such as voice over IP, which need traffic redirected onto a backup in tens of milliseconds. That is achievable by computing and signaling backups in advance of failure and by redirecting traffic as close to the failure as possible. The redirection then includes no path computation and no delay for failure notifications to travel between routers.

The methods apply only to explicitly-routed LSPs. LSPs whose routes change dynamically, such as those used in unicast IGP routing, are outside the scope.

The background section explains why there are two methods. Before this work began, operational networks had deployed two independent fast reroute methods, and vendors trying to support both ran into compatibility problems. The document does not pick a winner. It standardizes the RSVP signaling so that any implementation can recognize all fast reroute requests and either perform the method or return a clear error.
sections.eli5: Some traffic, like a phone call, cannot wait while routers figure out a new route. So the plan is to prepare the detour first and use it the instant something breaks.

sections.title: One-to-One and Facility Backup
sections.content:
In one-to-one backup, each router that can act as a point of local repair (PLR) computes a separate backup LSP, called a detour, for every LSP it protects. The detour rejoins the protected LSP downstream of the failure at a merge point (MP). Protecting an LSP through N nodes fully may need as many as (N - 1) detours. When a detour meets its protected LSP at a router with the same outgoing interface, the two are merged to keep the number of LSPs down. The label stack does not get deeper when a detour is used.

In facility backup, the PLR builds one bypass tunnel that protects a whole set of LSPs passing through the same facility. It uses the MPLS label stack: on failure the PLR swaps the label to one the merge point will understand as the protected LSP, then pushes the bypass tunnel's label. This scales better, because the same bypass tunnel can serve many LSPs, but it needs LSPs to share a common downstream node.

A bypass tunnel can be an NHOP tunnel, which bypasses one link, or an NNHOP tunnel, which bypasses a node.
sections.eli5: One way is to give every car its own personal detour map. The other is to build one shared side road that many cars can use at once.

sections.title: New RSVP Objects and Flags
sections.content:
Two new objects are added, and both can only be carried in RSVP Path messages. The FAST_REROUTE object (Class-Num 205, C-Type 1) is inserted only by the head-end and MUST NOT be changed downstream. It carries the setup and hold priorities (0 to 7, where 0 is highest), a hop-limit, flags, a bandwidth estimate, and three 32-bit attribute filters: include-any, exclude-any and include-all. The flags request 0x01 one-to-one backup or 0x02 facility backup. Routers that do not recognize the object ignore it and pass it on.

The DETOUR object (Class-Num 63, C-Type 7 for IPv4 and 8 for IPv6) lists one or more pairs of a PLR address and the downstream node it is trying to avoid. A router that does not support it MUST reject the Path message and send a PathErr.

The SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object gains two flags, 0x08 bandwidth protection desired and 0x10 node protection desired. The record-route (RRO) sub-objects gain 0x04 bandwidth protection and 0x08 node protection, which let a PLR report back what it was able to provide.
sections.eli5: The head-end writes its wishes on a request form: how important the traffic is, how much room it needs, and which style of detour it likes. Each router along the way ticks boxes to say what it can offer.

sections.title: Head-End and PLR Behavior
sections.content:
The head-end decides whether an LSP needs protection. It MUST either set the local protection desired flag or include a FAST_REROUTE object, or both, and SHOULD always set the flag. It MUST set label recording desired, which helps facility backup. If it wants a particular method, it includes a FAST_REROUTE object with the matching flag. If neither flag is set, or there is no object, PLRs treat that as no preference.

Every router on a protected LSP except the egress follows the PLR rules. Before computing a backup path, it collects the downstream nodes, the links and nodes to protect against, the upstream links, the attribute filters, the bandwidth and the hop-limit. The backup must avoid the protected link or node, must satisfy the resource requirements, and for a detour must end at the tail-end of the protected LSP. If the PLR is the penultimate hop, node protection is not possible.

The PLR also reports status in the RRO. It sets local protection available when a backup path exists and local protection in use only when it is actively redirecting traffic. When failure happens, the PLR sends a PathErr with error code 25 (Notify) and sub-code 3, "Tunnel locally repaired", so the head-end can compute a better path.
sections.eli5: The traveler says "I want a detour if anything breaks." Each stop along the road works out its own detour, tells the traveler whether it has one, and warns them when it has started using it.

sections.title: Merging and Reverting
sections.content:
A router should always assume it is a merge point, because under facility backup it may not know until a failure that a backup is arriving. Path messages for backups can be merged when they leave by the same interface to the same next hop. If one of them is for the protected LSP, the protected LSP's Path message is the one forwarded. In the path-specific method, merging is REQUIRED, and the merged DETOUR object combines all the (PLR_ID, Avoid_Node_ID) pairs.

When a downstream router sees a link fail, it must not clear Path and Resv state or send PathTear or ResvErr immediately, or facility backup would not work. It resets refresh timers so the PLR has time to start refreshing state over the bypass tunnel. State is still removed if it is not refreshed before the timer expires.

After repair, two strategies restore a full path. In global revertive mode, the head-end re-optimizes the tunnel, and the RFC says this SHOULD always be used. In local revertive mode, which is optional, the PLR re-signals LSPs over the restored resource. Because flapping resources could cause repeated disruption, a PLR using local revert should dampen the re-signaling.
sections.eli5: Where a detour rejoins the main road, the traffic officers there must expect it. Nobody should rip up the old road signs the moment it closes. And once the road reopens, the head office decides whether everyone should switch back.

sections.title: Security and Registry Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC states that it does not introduce new security issues, and the considerations of the original RSVP protocol remain relevant. One addition: facility backup requires a PLR and its chosen merge point to trust the RSVP messages they receive from each other.

For the IANA section, class number 63 is assigned to DETOUR with C-Types 7 (IPv4) and 8 (IPv6), and class number 205 to FAST_REROUTE with C-Type 1 and C-Type 7 reserved because pre-standard implementations still use it. For both, C-Types 0 through 127 are assigned by Standards Action, 128 through 191 by Expert Review, and 192 through 255 are reserved for Vendor Private Use.
sections.eli5: The only extra rule is that the two routers at each end of a shortcut have to trust each other's messages.

fields.name: Hop-limit
fields.desc: Maximum extra hops for the backup path between PLR and MP.

fields.name: Bandwidth
fields.desc: Estimate as a 32-bit IEEE floating point number, in bytes per second.

fields.name: Include-any
fields.desc: Attribute filters, any of which makes a link acceptable.

fields.name: Exclude-any
fields.desc: Attribute filters, any of which makes a link unacceptable.

fields.name: Include-all
fields.desc: Attribute filters, all of which must be present.

viz.caption: SESSION_ATTRIBUTE FLAGS (FIRST THREE EXISTING, LAST TWO NEW IN RFC 4090)

items.label: Local protection desired
items.desc: Transit routers may use local repair that violates the explicit route.

items.label: Label recording desired
items.desc: Label information should be included in the route record.

items.label: SE Style desired
items.desc: The ingress may reroute the tunnel without tearing it down.

items.label: Bandwidth protection desired
items.desc: A backup with a bandwidth guarantee is wanted.

items.label: Node protection desired
items.desc: A backup that bypasses at least the next node is wanted.
